title: India's Higher Education Sector
subtitle: A Decade of Growth, Access, and Inclusion
body_text:
Building India’s Knowledge Ecosystem: A Decade of Progress
Higher education is a cornerstone of India’s journey towards a knowledge-based economy and a key pillar of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 . The policy envisions an education system that promotes holistic, multidisciplinary learning and advances the goals of SDG 4. Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 focuses on ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and promoting lifelong learning opportunities for all. The Ministry of Education conducts an annual survey of Higher Education Institutions in India.
The All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE), conducted annually by the Ministry of Education, provides a comprehensive evidence base on Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) across the country. The data helps track the progress of higher education reforms under NEP 2020, identify emerging gaps, and inform policy responses.
A Growing Higher Education Footprint
According to AISHE reports, India’s higher education network has expanded significantly over the decade.
The number of universities increased from 760 in 2014–15 to 1,289 in 2023–24, representing a growth of 69.6 % . The number of colleges rose from 38,498 to 48,246 , an increase of 25.3% . Standalone institutions increased from 12,276 to 15,221 , registering about 24% growth.
This expansion reflects a widening institutional base and greater capacity to serve learners across the country. It has strengthened the reach of higher education, supported broader participation, and contributed to building a more accessible, diverse, and inclusive knowledge ecosystem for India’s future .
Increasing Student Enrolment: Advancing Equity and Inclusion
Higher education enrolment in India has risen steadily over the past decade, growing 31.5% from 3.42 crore students in 2014–15 to 4.50 crore in 2023–24.
The Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in higher education rose from 23.7% in 2014–15 to 29.5% in 2022–23, and further to 30% in 2023–24. This steady increase reflects growing access to and participation in higher education, supporting NEP 2020's target of raising the GER to 50% by 2035.
From 2014-15 to 2023-24 , level-wise percentage increase in total enrolments was: Ph.D 1.17 lakh to 3.43 lakh (192.89%); Post Graduate 38.53 lakh to 57.85 lakh (50.15%); Under Graduate 2.71 crore to 3.45 crore (27.27%); Diploma 25.08 lakh to 33.15 lakh (32.22%); Certificate 1.70 lakh to 2.08 lakh (22.55%); Integrated 1.41 lakh to 5.69 lakh (301.36%).
Female enrolment in higher education has witnessed steady growth over the past decade. It grew by 42.2% , rising from 1.57 crore in 2014–15 to 2.24 crore in 2023–24 , outpacing the growth in total enrolment during the decade. The number of female students enrolled in various courses in 2023-24 was: Ph.D: 1.71 lakh ; Post-Graduate: 32.53 lakh ; Under Graduate: 1.71 crore PG Diploma: 91,332 ; Diploma: 13.27 lakh ; Certificate: 1.10 lakh , and Integrated: 2.73 lakh . Female GER increased from 22.9% in 2014–15 to 31.2% in 2023–24 , surpassing male GER (28.9%) for the seventh consecutive year. Higher education out-turn increased from 88.28 lakh in 2014–15 to over 1.09 crore in 2023–24 a 24.06% increase. The growth reflects improved programme completion, enhanced retention, rising enrolment, and expanded institutional capacity. Supported by government initiatives, this trend highlights progress in access, equity, quality, and performance in higher education.
Higher education out-turn refers to the total number of students who pass out of higher education institutions in a given academic year.
Gender Parity Index (GPI) in higher education improved significantly, rising from 0.92 in 2014–15 to 1.08 in 2023–24. GPI for the SC category increased from 0.91 to 1.11 , while ST category GPI rose from 0.81 to 1.08 during the same period. The rising GPI points to increasing parity favoring females. The progress highlights the impact of government initiatives in promoting equity , inclusion , and balanced participation in higher education.
​​​​​​​
Gender Parity Index (GPI) The Gender Parity Index (GPI) is the ratio of GER for females to GER for males, reflecting equitable participation of females in the education system. A GPI of 1 indicates parity between the sexes. A GPI between 0 and 1 typically indicates a disparity favoring males. A GPI greater than 1 indicates a disparity favoring females.
The share of SC enrolment rose from 13.44% in 2014–15 to 15.5% in 2023–24 in total enrolment.  During the same period, the share of ST enrolment increased from 4.8% to 6.4% . OBC participation climbed from 32.8% to 40.1%, registering the largest increase in enrolment share among all social categories. The GER for SC students increased from 18.9% in 2014–15 to 27.8% in 2023–24 . For the ST students, it increased from 13.5% in 2014–15 to 22.8% in 2023–24 . Increasing participation of students from SC, ST and OBC categories reflects growing inclusivity in higher education.
Persons with Benchmark Disability (PwBD) enrolment increased from 64,298 in 2014–15 to 88,816 in 2022–23, registering a growth of 38.1%. Male and female enrolment grew by 54.4% and 19.0% , respectively, during this period. In 2023–24, 54,080 PwBD students were enrolled, including 34,080 males and 20,000 females . Higher male enrolment among PwBD points to a persistent gender imbalance in access to higher education. This suggests that improvements in access have not translated equally across genders.
Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) Enrolment
Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) enrolments in higher education have increased steadily over the past decade.
Total enrolments increased from 91.5 lakh in 2014–15 to 1.02 crore in 2023–24, representing an overall increase of approximately 11.5% over the period.
The growth reflects expanding institutional capacity and sustained student interest in STEM disciplines, driven by government initiatives, digital technologies, innovation, research, and employment opportunities strengthening India's knowledge economy.
Foreign Student Enrolment in Higher Education
Foreign student enrolment rose from 42,293 in 2014–15 to 58,134 in 2023–24, an increase of approximately 37.5% over the past decade — reflecting India's growing appeal as a destination for higher learning among international students. This points to the growing internationalisation of higher education, enhanced academic collaborations and global recognition of Indian institutions.
Faculty Growth in Higher Education
The number of teachers in higher education increased from 14.73 lakh in 2014–15 to 17.32 lakh in 2023–24 , representing an overall increase of 2.59 lakh teachers , or approximately 17.6% growth during the period.
The absolute number of female teachers grew by 36.7% between 2014–15 and 2023–24, reflecting growing equity in employment opportunities for women in the sector. In both 2022–23 and 2023–24, the share of male teachers in the total teaching workforce remained higher than that of female teachers. In 2022-23, the share of female teachers was 44.3%. It grew marginally to 44.9% in 2023-24.
Infrastructure facilities
Between 2014–15 and 2023–24, infrastructure facilities in higher education institutions have improved considerably. Physical and digital infrastructure, green infrastructure and separate amenities for women and PwBD have been developed across institutions. In 2023–24:
94% of universities, 95% of colleges, and 91% of standalone institutions had a playground. 98% of universities, 98% of colleges, and 98% of standalone institutions had a library facility. 89% of universities, 85% of colleges, and 94% of standalone institutions had a laboratory.
In addition, most universities, colleges, and standalone institutions were also equipped with facilities such as health centres, skill development and computer centres, auditoriums, and conference halls.
Towards a Future-Ready Higher Education Ecosystem
India’s higher education sector has expanded significantly over the past decade, with growth in institutions, enrolment, faculty strength and student out-turn. Improvements in Gross Enrolment Ratio, women’s participation, gender parity, and inclusion of SC, ST and other disadvantaged groups reflect enhanced access and equity. Rising enrolment in STEM and international students indicates the strengthening of India's knowledge ecosystem. Together, these achievements highlight the impact of NEP 2020 in promoting quality, inclusion, and excellence.

enrichment.summary: This PIB backgrounder presents a decade-long (2014-15 to 2023-24) overview of India's higher education sector based on AISHE data, highlighting growth in institutions, enrolment, and inclusion under NEP 2020. Universities grew 69.6% to 1,289, enrolment rose 31.5% to 4.50 crore, and Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) increased from 23.7% to 30%. Female GER (31.2%) surpassed male GER for the seventh consecutive year, and Gender Parity Index improved to 1.08, alongside gains in SC/ST/OBC participation, STEM enrolment, foreign student numbers, and faculty strength.
enrichment.context:
The All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE) is the Ministry of Education's annual flagship survey providing the primary statistical evidence base for tracking higher education indicators like GER, GPI, and enrolment by social category, gender and discipline. It is central to monitoring NEP 2020 implementation, particularly the ambitious target of raising GER to 50% by 2035 — a benchmark far from being met given the current 30% figure, indicating substantial ground still to cover. NEP 2020 itself, adopted in 2020, replaced the 1986 policy framework and emphasizes multidisciplinary education, flexible curricula (via mechanisms like the Academic Bank of Credits and multiple entry-exit points), and equity-focused interventions such as the Higher Education Financing Agency (HEFA), scholarships, and the establishment of institutions in aspirational and underserved districts.

The data on Gender Parity Index (GPI) crossing 1.0 for women overall and for SC/ST categories is significant because it signals a reversal of historical gender gaps in Indian higher education, though this must be read alongside continuing disparities in PwBD (Persons with Benchmark Disability) enrolment, where male participation still substantially outpaces female participation. Such AISHE-based reports are frequently used by UPSC to test understanding of educational statistics, government scheme outcomes (RUSA, SIRF, PMSSS for foreign/domestic students), and the broader SDG 4 framework on inclusive and equitable quality education, making familiarity with key trend figures useful for both Prelims data-based questions and Mains essays on education policy and social equity.

prelims_questions.question:
With reference to the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) in India's higher education sector, consider the following statements:
1. The GER increased from 23.7% in 2014-15 to 30% in 2023-24.
2. NEP 2020 targets a GER of 50% by 2035.
3. Female GER has remained lower than male GER throughout the decade 2014-24.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: As per AISHE data cited in the release, GER rose from 23.7% to 30% and NEP 2020 targets 50% GER by 2035. However, female GER (31.2%) has surpassed male GER (28.9%) for the seventh consecutive year, making statement 3 incorrect.

prelims_questions.question: The Gender Parity Index (GPI) in education is defined as:
options: The ratio of literacy rate of females to males
The ratio of GER for females to GER for males
The ratio of female teachers to male teachers
The ratio of female enrolment to total enrolment
prelims_questions.explanation: As stated in the release, GPI is the ratio of GER for females to GER for males; a value greater than 1 indicates disparity favoring females, as seen in India's 2023-24 figure of 1.08.

mains_questions.question: Examine the trends in Gross Enrolment Ratio and Gender Parity Index in India's higher education sector over the last decade. Discuss the extent to which these trends reflect the goals of NEP 2020 and SDG 4, and identify areas requiring further policy attention.

Despite improvements in overall access and gender parity in higher education, certain groups such as Persons with Benchmark Disability continue to face uneven participation. Discuss the structural barriers to inclusive higher education in India and suggest measures to address them.

study_notes.reason: The release carries a strong testable factual core (AISHE data, GER/GPI definitions and figures, NEP 2020 targets) as well as genuine analytical material on equity gaps (PwBD gender disparity, GER shortfall against NEP target) that would support a Mains answer.

prelims.point: AISHE (All India Survey on Higher Education) is conducted annually by the Ministry of Education and is the primary data source for GER, GPI and enrolment statistics.
prelims.why_important: UPSC frequently frames statement-based questions around which body/agency conducts a given survey.

prelims.point: Gender Parity Index (GPI) = ratio of female GER to male GER; GPI=1 indicates parity, GPI>1 favours females, GPI between 0-1 favours males.
prelims.why_important: A precise definitional distinction UPSC could test via a statement on interpretation of GPI values.

prelims.point: India's GER in higher education rose from 23.7% (2014-15) to 30% (2023-24); NEP 2020 targets 50% GER by 2035.
prelims.why_important: A core statistic and target frequently used in prelims data-comparison questions on education policy.

prelims.point: Female GER (31.2%) has surpassed male GER (28.9%) for the seventh consecutive year in 2023-24.
prelims.why_important: A specific trend fact that could appear as a standalone statement to verify.

prelims.point: Number of universities grew from 760 to 1,289 (69.6% growth) between 2014-15 and 2023-24.
prelims.why_important: A quantifiable institutional growth figure that could be tested against other growth percentages given in the release.

prelims.point: NEP 2020 replaced the 1986 education policy and introduced mechanisms like Academic Bank of Credits and multiple entry-exit points.
prelims.why_important: A key policy feature likely to be tested on NEP 2020's distinguishing provisions.

mains.point: Despite overall GER improvement to 30%, India remains far short of the NEP 2020 target of 50% by 2035, indicating substantial structural gaps in access to higher education.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for 'Examine the progress and challenges in achieving NEP 2020 targets' type questions.

mains.point: While overall GPI and SC/ST GPI have crossed 1.0 favouring females, PwBD enrolment shows a persistent gender imbalance with male participation substantially higher, showing uneven translation of equity gains across marginalised groups.
mains.analytical_use: Supports 'Critically examine whether gains in gender parity in Indian education are uniformly distributed across social groups' type questions.

mains.point: Rising SC/ST/OBC enrolment shares and GER growth reflect the impact of affirmative and inclusion-focused policies, but growth rates vary significantly across categories (OBC largest share increase).
mains.analytical_use: Can be used in 'Discuss the role of reservation and targeted schemes in improving higher education access for disadvantaged groups' answers.

mains.point: Growth in STEM enrolment and foreign student numbers signals strengthening of India's knowledge economy and internationalisation of higher education, relevant to India's soft power and human capital strategy.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on India's aspirations to become a global education hub or knowledge economy.

mains.point: Female teacher share in higher education remains below 45% despite growth, indicating continuing gender gap in academic employment even as student-side parity improves.
mains.analytical_use: Supports analysis distinguishing progress in student enrolment equity versus faculty employment equity.

low_priority.point: Detailed infrastructure percentages (playgrounds, libraries, laboratories) across institution types.
low_priority.reason: Descriptive administrative detail with no analytical or testable significance beyond generic access indicators.

low_priority.point: Level-wise enrolment growth percentages (Ph.D, PG, UG, Diploma, Certificate, Integrated).
low_priority.reason: Granular statistics unlikely to be individually tested and not analytically significant beyond overall enrolment trend already captured.

low_priority.point: Rhetorical framing about 'Building India's Knowledge Ecosystem' and NEP vision statements.
low_priority.reason: General promotional language without specific policy substance.
